summary: Children learn the four human tooth types (incisors, canines, premolars, molars) and the organising idea that TOOTH SHAPE IS LINKED TO FUNCTION: flat-edged incisors cut/bite, pointed canines tear, and broad bumpy premolars and molars grind. The anchor is the child's own mouth as evidence — feeling sharp front teeth versus wide bumpy back teeth — paired with linking each shape to a demonstrable action on food. The idea is extended and tested across animals (herbivore flat grinders, carnivore sharp tearers) and lands on humans as omnivores who have ALL types because we eat both plants and meat. The animal comparison is treated as reasoning/evidence for the rule, not a separate fact to memorise.
misconceptions: 'All teeth are the same / just different sizes' — missing that different shapes do different jobs.
'Canines/'fangs' are for biting food hardest' — conflating pointiness with power; canines TEAR, the flat molars do the heavy grinding.
'Front teeth grind and back teeth cut' — reversing the position–function mapping.
'Carnivores have flat teeth because they're big animals' — linking tooth shape to size rather than to diet.
'Humans have special teeth unlike animals' — missing that we share the same tooth types and that having all of them marks us as omnivores.
'Teeth grow back if lost' at this age — confusing the one milk-to-adult replacement with unlimited regrowth (a common aside worth correcting).

activities.title: Feel and map your own teeth
steps: Run your tongue along the front teeth, then the back teeth, and notice the difference: sharp flat front edges versus wide bumpy back surfaces; look with a mirror if available.
On a mouth/jaw map, locate and name the four types grouped by position: incisors and canines at the front, premolars and molars toward the back.
For each type, say what it does when eating: incisor = cut/slice, canine = grip and tear, premolar/molar = crush and grind.
activities.insight: Teeth are not all the same — different shapes at different positions do different jobs, and you can feel this evidence in your own mouth.

activities.title: Apple-eating sequence: which tooth does which job
steps: Watch or describe eating a bite of apple and identify which teeth do each step: incisors slice in, then premolars and molars crush and grind.
Match each tooth type to the food-action it performs (cut, tear, grind).
Explain why the flat back molars — not the pointed canines — do the heavy grinding.
activities.insight: The job a tooth does follows from its shape: thin edges cut, points tear, flat bumpy surfaces grind.

activities.title: Predict an animal's teeth from its diet
steps: Before seeing the answer, predict what a grass-eating animal's teeth look like and what a meat-eating animal's teeth look like, and say why.

Check predictions against examples: a herbivore (e.g. a sheep or cow) with mostly flat wide cheek teeth for grinding tough plants; a carnivore (e.g. a lion) with sharp pointed tearers. (Notes: a rabbit is a herbivore too, but also has large front incisors for gnawing, so sheep and cow show the flat-grinder pattern most clearly; the fox is often used as a simple meat-eater but is actually a dietary omnivore, so the lion is the cleaner carnivore example.)

Answer a probe such as: a cow has no teeth at all at the front top of its mouth (just a hard pad) and no sharp pointed tearing teeth — what does that tell you it probably does NOT eat? And why would sharp tearing teeth be no good for an animal eating grass all day?
activities.insight: Tooth shape matches the job the diet needs, so you can reason from a diet to likely teeth (and from teeth back to likely diet).

activities.title: Read your own diet off your own teeth: why humans are omnivores
steps: Note that your mouth has BOTH sharp pointed front teeth AND flat wide back teeth.
Reason backwards: having both tooth shapes is evidence that both kinds of food can be eaten — eating both plants and meat is what 'omnivore' means.
Explain why humans have all four tooth types, connecting it to eating both plants and meat.

Answer the two-tier prompt: 'A sheep eats plants such as grass and a lion eats meat — would their teeth look the same or different, and why? And what does it tell you that humans have both sharp front teeth and flat back teeth?'
activities.insight: Humans share the same tooth types as many other mammals; having all of them is evidence we are omnivores who eat both plants and meat — the punchline that ties diet, teeth and the animal comparison together.

checkQuestion: A sheep eats only grass and a fox eats meat. If you looked inside their mouths, would their teeth look the same or different? Explain why. And what does it tell you that humans have BOTH sharp pointed teeth at the front AND flat wide teeth at the back?
checkAnswer: Different: the sheep (a herbivore) has mostly flat, wide teeth for grinding tough grass; the fox (a carnivore) has sharp, pointed teeth for tearing meat — tooth SHAPE matches the JOB the diet needs. Humans have both kinds because we are omnivores who eat plants and meat, so we need incisors and canines to cut and tear AND premolars and molars to grind.
